name: Ikizu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Aunio, Robinson, Roth, Stegen & Allison. 2019. The Mara languages (JE40). In Van de Velde et al. (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 2nd ed. Routledge. Paywalled.
earlier_scan.note: Mara Bantu chapter covers Ikizu tone system; not openly fetchable

new_statements.quote: The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme [...] Ikizu also assigns tones to moras but counts syllables. [...] In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult, and in Ikizu, the lexical tone spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. [...] Ikizu has two tonal patterns for monosyllabic noun stems and three patterns for longer stems (Table 7), with H spreading to the end of the stem. [...] in Ikizu the three underlying patterns are ØØØ, HØØ, and ØHØ. However, Ikizu toneless patterns are realised with a stem-initial H when the noun is pronounced in isolation.
new_statements.citation: Aunio, Lotta, Holly Robinson, Tim Roth, Oliver Stegen & John B. Walker. 2019. The Mara languages (JE40). In Van de Velde, Bostoen, Nurse & Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn, 501-532. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure' and the nominal-tone paragraph with Table 7 'Ikizu nominal tones' (accepted-manuscript pdf pp. 7 and 9; print pp. 501-532, exact print page not seen)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikizu is described as a privative-H tone language, not a stress language: noun stems are lexically toneless, penult-H or antepenult-H (Table 7: ùmù-ɾìmì 'farmer' / òmò-ɾámú 'brother-in-law' / ùmú-βísá 'enemy'), with the H spreading rightward to the end of the stem except onto an utterance-final syllable; toneless nouns get a stem-initial H in isolation; the Infinitive H sits on the antepenult of the macrostem. No source opened makes any statement about word stress in Ikizu; the chapter's only 'penultimate stress' remark concerns Zanaki.
new_statements.exceptions: Ikizu allows contour tones 'in some restricted contexts'; the toneless/H contrast of nouns is neutralised in isolation (stem-initial H inserted). Orthography Statement p. 9 adds that phonemic long vowels in noun stems occur almost exclusively in the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Nominal tone is stated for the stem and for phrase-medial vs utterance-final (isolation) forms; verb melodies are stated for the macrostem. No word-stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ikizu proper (JE402, [ikz]) as spoken in Bunda/Musoma districts; the SIL orthography covers Ikizu-Sizaki jointly (Sizaki [szk] was merged into ikz by ISO change request 2007-033). The Mara chapter's Ikizu data are the same SIL/Helsinki corpus used by Aunio & Robinson.

sources.note: Ikizu named only in the list of JE40 languages (draft p. 3); all data are Ikoma-Nata-Isenye and Ngoreme. General remark that these restricted-tone systems combine tone- and stress-like features (obligatoriness) but are not stress systems; nothing on Ikizu.

sources.citation: Robinson, Holly (author). 2016. Ikizu-Sizaki Orthography Statement, Approved Orthography Edition, April 2016. SIL International, Uganda-Tanzania Branch. 64 pp. (updated version of Gray & Smith 2010 Ikizu Orthography Sketch)
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tone, p. 19: 'Ikizu has lexical tone on nouns, but this tone does not have a high functional load and therefore is not written in the orthography... Ikizu also has a variety of grammatical tone melodies, but none of them are contrastive.' Sec. 2.1.2, p. 9: in noun stems phonemic long vowels occur 'almost exclusively in the penultimate syllable'. No stress or accent statement.

sources.citation: Aunio, Lotta. 2015. A typological perspective on Bantu nominal tone: the case of Ikoma-Nata-Isenye in western Tanzania. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 33(3): 359-371. doi:10.2989/16073614.2015.1105106 [Helda accepted manuscript]
sources.note: Draft pdf p. 12 (print c. p. 368), one paragraph on Ikizu: aligns nominal lexical tones to the right edge of the stem; nouns are toneless (umu-ɾimi 'farmer') or have penult H (omo-ɾámu) or antepenult H (umú-βisa); systematic rightward H spread except utterance-finally; toneless utterances not allowed, so toneless nouns get an antepenultimate or stem-initial H in isolation; phrase-medially [-Oblig(H)] [-Culm(H)]. No stress statement.

sources.note: Sec. 2 phonology sketch (pp. 9-12); sec. 2.3 Tone, p. 12: 'Ikizu is a tonal language, with initial research revealing two tone patterns for nouns in isolation and a single tone pattern on verbs... Tone is not marked on any data in this paper.' Sec. 2.2: contrastive vowel length (two degrees). No mention of stress or accent.
